dedupe_keys.name: historic landfills in england climate change and pollution risk to rivers and groundwater brand and spencer wires water

description: This review article looks at how climate change could raise the pollution risk from England's historic landfills, the many old tips that predate modern regulation and were never sealed off from their surroundings. Following an earlier WIREs Water article that analysed historic landfills at risk from coastal flooding and erosion across England, this update turns to inland sites. More frequent and larger river floods would increase leachate and the chance that floodwater erodes a landfill and releases waste; drought can crack capping and open new pathways; and changes in groundwater can carry leachate to water supplies, since thousands of historic landfills sit in groundwater Source Protection Zones where they would not be allowed today. The authors warn of costs for drinking water treatment and of tipping points where rivers already face other pressures, and they call for work on risk prioritisation and remediation. The article is free to read and download as open access under CC BY in WIREs Water. Coverage is England. Caveats: a review and scoping analysis, not a site-by-site risk dataset; facts here come from the abstract. Simulation uses: hazard pathways and receptors for modelling legacy landfill failures under flood and drought scenarios. Related records: the Environment Agency historic landfill sites dataset (data-ea-historic-landfill-sites) and the coastal historic landfills data (data-historic-coastal-landfills-crown-estate) hold the sites themselves.

name: Historic landfills in England: climate change and pollution risk to rivers and groundwater (Brand and Spencer, WIREs Water)
outcomes: Argues that more frequent and larger river floods will increase leachate generation and the chance of landfill erosion and waste release, that drought can crack capping and open new pathways, and that thousands of historic landfills lie in groundwater Source Protection Zones; calls for research on contaminant behaviour, receptor vulnerability, risk prioritisation and remediation.
